turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for seeing me. I hope I'm not taking up too much of your busy day. 

Well... I came in because the ladies at my church thought it would be best if I talked to someone. I guess I've been doing some... well, just some slightly odd things lately. Nothing bad, I promise! It's just... at the church dinners, by the potluck table, I'll pick up the serving spoon and then I just... I kind of freeze. I'll just stand there holding the spoon up in the air, not moving at all. Or... or I'll stand there and fold the exact same stack of napkins over and over again, even when folks are waiting on me to move along. 

I really don't mean to hold up the line or be a nuisance to anyone. I just get a little stuck, I suppose. Does that make sense, Doctor? I hope I'm explaining it alright for you.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing in place while holding a spoon and repetitively folding the same stack of napkins, which are examples of disorganized or abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: When you keep folding the same stack of napkins over and over, do you feel like you have to do it to relieve a strong inner urge?

Oh, no, Doctor, it’s nothing like that. I promise I don't have any... any strong urges or anything bad like that. It’s not like I feel anxious or forced to do it. 

I just... my hands just sort of keep going on their own, I suppose. I don't really even realize I'm doing it until one of the ladies gently taps my shoulder. It’s just a silly little habit, really, nothing for anyone to worry about. Am I answering your question alright? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes their repetitive napkin folding as an automatic action where their hands 'keep going on their own' without realization, indicating disorganized or abnormal motor behavior (stereotypy).
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies feeling anxious, forced, or having any strong inner urges to perform the repetitive behavior, ruling out compulsions.
